questions.explanation: Mixing two secondaries such as orange and green neutralises the hues into a greyish (tertiary) colour; red and blue give purple and white and red give pink.

questions.explanation: Perspective represents depth and distance on a flat surface.

questions.stem:
Explain any three of the following:
(a) rhythm; [5 marks]
(b) balance; [5 marks]
(c) harmony; [5 marks]
(d) symmetry. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: First term correctly explained (meaning 2, how it is achieved/types 2, example 1); e.g. rhythm - repetition of elements creating visual movement
5 marks: Second term correctly explained (meaning 2, how achieved/types 2, example 1); e.g. balance - equal distribution of visual weight; formal/symmetrical, informal/asymmetrical, radial
5 marks: Third term correctly explained (meaning 2, how achieved/types 2, example 1); e.g. harmony - pleasing agreement of related elements; symmetry - identical arrangement on both sides of a central axis
questions.explanation: Rhythm is the regular or ordered repetition of lines, shapes, colours or motifs that leads the eye through a work and gives it a sense of movement, e.g. repeated motifs on an adire cloth; it may be regular, alternating, flowing or progressive. Balance is the even distribution of visual weight in a composition so that no part appears heavier than another; it may be formal (symmetrical), informal (asymmetrical) or radial. Harmony is the pleasing unity achieved when related elements - similar colours, shapes or textures - are combined so that the parts agree with one another, e.g. using analogous colours. Symmetry is the exact correspondence of form on opposite sides of a central dividing line, such that one half mirrors the other, as in a frontal mask or the human face.

questions.stem:
(a) What is Theatre Arts? [1 mark]
(b) State three characteristics of Theatre Arts [6 marks]
(c) Outline any four significance of Theatre Arts to the society. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Theatre arts: the performing art of presenting stories/ideas live before an audience through acting, dialogue, music, dance and spectacle
2 marks: (b) Characteristic 1: performed live before an audience
2 marks: (b) Characteristic 2: involves actors/characters, dialogue and action (plot)
2 marks: (b) Characteristic 3: uses visual art elements - stage, scenery, costume, make-up, props, lighting - with music and dance
2 marks: (c) Entertainment and relaxation
2 marks: (c) Education/enlightenment and moral instruction
2 marks: (c) Preservation and transmission of culture and history
2 marks: (c) Social criticism/correction, job creation and income, promotion of unity and tourism (any relevant)
questions.explanation: (a) Theatre arts is the performing art in which stories, ideas or events are presented live before an audience through acting, speech, music, dance and visual spectacle. (b) It is performed live in front of an audience; it involves characters, dialogue and action arranged in a plot; and it combines other arts - scenery, costumes, make-up, props, lighting, music and dance. (c) It entertains and relaxes people; it educates and gives moral instruction; it preserves and passes on culture, history and tradition; it criticises and corrects social ills; and it creates employment for actors, designers and technicians and promotes tourism and national unity.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem:
Write notes on Igbo Ukwu art under the following headings:
(a) location; [2 marks]
(b) archeological sites; [3 marks]
(c) art forms; [6 marks]
(d) characteristics. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Igbo Ukwu, a town in Anambra State, south-eastern Nigeria (near Awka/Onitsha); discovered 1938 by Isaiah Anozie, excavated by Thurstan Shaw 1959-60; c. 9th-10th century AD
1 mark: (b) Igbo Isaiah - a storehouse/shrine of regalia
1 mark: (b) Igbo Richard - burial chamber of a priest-king (Eze Nri)
1 mark: (b) Igbo Jonah - a disposal pit/cache
6 marks: (c) Any six art forms, 1 mark each: roped (water) pot; bronze bowls and vessels; shell-shaped vessel/bronze shell; altar stand; pendants and ornaments; staff/fly-whisk handles; leopard skull/head; beads and bangles; crown/regalia
1 mark: (d) Leaded bronze cast by the lost-wax (cire perdue) process
1 mark: (d) Very intricate, delicate surface decoration and fine granulation
1 mark: (d) Motifs of insects and reptiles - flies, beetles, snakes, frogs, grasshoppers
1 mark: (d) Thin walls, small size and decorative rather than naturalistic style
questions.explanation: (a) Igbo Ukwu is a town in Anambra State, south-eastern Nigeria, near Awka and Onitsha. Its bronzes were found accidentally in 1938 by Isaiah Anozie while digging a cistern and were excavated by Professor Thurstan Shaw in 1959-60; they date to about the 9th-10th century AD. (b) The three sites are Igbo Isaiah (a storehouse/shrine of ritual objects), Igbo Richard (the burial chamber of a priest-king, probably an Eze Nri) and Igbo Jonah (a disposal pit). (c) Art forms include the famous roped pot, bronze bowls and vessels, a bronze shell, an altar stand, pendants, staff and fly-whisk handles, a leopard skull, bracelets, crowns and thousands of glass and stone beads. (d) The works are of leaded bronze cast by the lost-wax process; they are small, thin-walled and covered with extremely intricate decoration and granulation, with insect and reptile motifs such as flies, beetles, snakes and frogs; the style is decorative rather than naturalistic.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem:
Discuss Kissi art under the following headings:
(a) location; [2 marks]
(b) art forms; [3 marks]
(c) characteristics. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Kissi people of the border area of Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia (mainly south-eastern Guinea)
3 marks: (b) Small soapstone (steatite) figures called pomdo (pl. pomtan), related to the nomoli; also heads and figures used as ancestor/spirit representations
2 marks: (c) Carved from soft soapstone (steatite); small in size
2 marks: (c) Large heads out of proportion to the body, with bulging eyes, broad flat nose and prominent lips
2 marks: (c) Figures often seated, squatting or kneeling, some holding objects; some bearded or wearing headgear
2 marks: (c) Smooth or weathered surfaces; many found buried in the ground and regarded as very old
2 marks: (c) Used in ancestor worship, kept on shrines and consulted as oracles or to protect crops and ensure good rice harvests
questions.explanation: (a) The Kissi live in south-eastern Guinea and the neighbouring border areas of Sierra Leone and Liberia. (b) Their best known art form is small stone figures carved from soapstone (steatite) called pomdo (plural pomtan), similar to the nomoli of the Mende; they include full figures and heads. (c) The figures are small and carved in soft soapstone; the head is very large in proportion to the body, with bulging eyes, a broad flat nose and thick protruding lips; many are shown seated, squatting or kneeling, sometimes bearded, wearing headgear or holding objects. Many are found buried in the soil and are believed to be very old, so their surfaces are often worn. The Kissi regard them as representations of ancestors: they are kept in shrines, wrapped in cloth, consulted as oracles and used to protect the farms and ensure good rice harvests.

questions.topic: Art of West Africa: general concepts
questions.stem: Discuss with examples, five roles of traditional arts of West Africa. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Religious/ritual role - objects for worship of gods and ancestors, e.g. shrine figures, Yoruba Ifa divination trays, Ashanti akuaba
3 marks: Social/ceremonial role - masks and costumes for festivals, initiation, funerals, e.g. Egungun, Gelede, Senufo masks
3 marks: Political role - symbols of authority and royalty, e.g. Benin bronzes, Ashanti stools and linguist staffs, beaded crowns
3 marks: Historical/record role - recording events and preserving history, e.g. Benin bronze plaques, Ife heads, commemorative heads
3 marks: Economic/utilitarian role - everyday objects and trade items, e.g. pottery, kente and adire cloth, calabashes, baskets; also education and entertainment
questions.explanation: Traditional art in West Africa served many purposes. (1) Religious: carvings, shrine figures and divination objects such as Yoruba Ifa trays, Ibeji twin figures and Ashanti akuaba dolls were used in worship of gods and ancestors. (2) Social and ceremonial: masks and costumes were used at festivals, initiation, funerals and masquerades, e.g. Egungun and Gelede masks of the Yoruba and Senufo and Dan masks. (3) Political: art symbolised authority and status, e.g. the Golden Stool and linguist staffs of the Ashanti, beaded crowns of Yoruba kings and Benin royal bronzes. (4) Historical: art recorded events and preserved history, e.g. Benin bronze plaques showing court life and wars, and commemorative heads of past kings. (5) Economic and utilitarian: pots, baskets, calabashes, kente and adire cloths and leatherwork served daily needs and were traded for income; art also educated the young and entertained the community.

questions.topic: Art of West Africa: general concepts
questions.stem:
(a) Name three media used in traditional African sculpture. [3 marks]
(b) Describe four characteristics of traditional African sculpture. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Any three media, 1 mark each: wood; terracotta/clay; bronze/brass; stone/soapstone; ivory; iron; mud
3 marks: (b) Frontality and symmetry - figures face forward and are bilaterally balanced
3 marks: (b) Disproportion/stylisation - large head (often a quarter to a third of the body), short legs; emphasis on what is important
3 marks: (b) Stylised, abstract and simplified forms rather than naturalism; static/rigid posture with bent knees
3 marks: (b) Smooth or decorated surfaces with scarification marks, symbolic motifs; mostly carved from a single block, made for religious/social functions
questions.explanation: (a) Traditional African sculptors worked in wood, terracotta (fired clay), bronze or brass, stone (including soapstone), ivory, iron and mud. (b) Characteristics: (1) Frontality and symmetry - figures face forward and the two sides mirror each other. (2) Disproportion - the head is usually very large (a quarter to a third of the figure) because it is regarded as the seat of life and wisdom, while the legs are short. (3) Stylisation and abstraction - forms are simplified and exaggerated rather than copied from nature, with rigid, static postures and slightly bent knees. (4) Surface treatment - surfaces are polished or decorated with scarification marks, hairstyles and symbolic patterns; works are usually carved from a single piece and made for religious, social or political purposes rather than for decoration alone.

questions.stem: Write an appreciation on "The last supper" [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Background: by Leonardo da Vinci (High Renaissance), c. 1495-1498, wall painting in the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan
3 marks: Subject matter: Christ's last meal with the twelve apostles at the moment he announces that one of them will betray him; their reactions
3 marks: Composition: one-point linear perspective with vanishing point at Christ's head; Christ in the centre as a stable triangle framed by the window; apostles in four groups of three; symmetrical balance
3 marks: Technique/medium: experimental tempera and oil on dry plaster (not true fresco), which led to early deterioration; chiaroscuro, realistic gestures and expressions
3 marks: Evaluation/significance: masterpiece of the High Renaissance showing psychological drama, unity and balance; widely copied and studied; restored in 1999
questions.explanation: The Last Supper is a mural painted by Leonardo da Vinci between about 1495 and 1498 on the wall of the refectory (dining hall) of the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy, and is a masterpiece of the High Renaissance. It shows Christ at his last meal with the twelve apostles at the dramatic moment he says, 'One of you will betray me'; the apostles react with shock, anger and questioning, while Judas draws back clutching a money bag. The composition is built on one-point perspective: all the lines of the ceiling and walls converge on Christ's head, placing him at the centre as a calm, stable triangle framed by the light of the window behind him. The apostles are arranged symmetrically in four groups of three, giving balance and rhythm. Leonardo used an experimental tempera and oil technique on dry plaster rather than true fresco, which caused the paint to flake soon after; the work has been restored several times, most recently in 1999. The gestures, expressions, lighting and perspective make it a powerful study of human emotion and one of the most famous paintings in the world.

questions.stem: In what five ways can the cave man be regarded as a creative person? [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Painted animals realistically on cave walls and ceilings, e.g. Lascaux (France) and Altamira (Spain)
3 marks: Produced his own colours/pigments from earth ochres, charcoal, animal fat and blood, and made brushes from fur, feathers and twigs; blew paint through hollow bones
3 marks: Used the natural bulges of the rock to give his figures volume and three-dimensional effect
3 marks: Carved figurines and reliefs in stone, bone and ivory, e.g. Venus of Willendorf
3 marks: Made tools, weapons, pottery and ornaments, built shelters/megaliths (e.g. Stonehenge) and engraved signs and symbols
questions.explanation: The cave man showed great creativity: (1) he painted lively, realistic animals such as bison, horses and deer on cave walls and ceilings, as at Lascaux in France and Altamira in Spain; (2) he made his own pigments from earth ochres, charcoal and burnt bones mixed with animal fat, blood or water, and made brushes from fur, feathers and chewed twigs, or blew paint through hollow bones to make stencilled hand prints; (3) he used the natural bulges and hollows of the rock surface to give his animals form and volume; (4) he carved figurines and reliefs in stone, bone and ivory, such as the Venus of Willendorf, and engraved designs on bones and antlers; (5) he made tools, weapons, pottery and ornaments and, in the Neolithic period, built houses and megalithic monuments such as Stonehenge.
